newsitem.title: CANADA: No quick deal seen in Falconbridge Canada strike.
newsitem.headline: No quick deal seen in Falconbridge Canada strike.

text.p: Unionized workers went on strike on Friday at Falconbridge Ltd.'s Sudbury, Ontario, mining operations, and analysts predicted the labour dispute would not be settled quickly.
About 1,400 unionized workers walked off the job Friday morning at Canada's second-biggest nickel miner after a last-ditch attempt to reach an agreement failed overnight.
"We bargained to the wire, but in the end the company's offer was short of the union's needs," said Rolly Gauthier, president of Local 598 of the Canadian Auto Workers union.
He said the talks broke down over wages, pensions and contract language.
Falconbridge said its final offer was similar to the agreement that ended Inco Ltd.'s 26-day strike at its Ontario operations last month.

"Unfortunately, at the end of the process the union was not prepared to recommend to our employees what we believe to be a very competitive and comprehensive offer," Falconbridge chief negotiator Gerald Foley said.
There was no indication when contract talks would resume.
Nickel gained $55 to $7,485 a metric ton on the London Metal Exchange on Friday, but some traders said the strike was already factored into the market.
Falconbridge's Sudbury operations last year produced 45,700 metric tons of nickel, 50,000 metric tons of copper and 1,600 metric tons of cobalt, including custom feed.
The mill and smelter have been in a planned maintenance shutdown since July 20, which was scheduled to end Aug. 5.

Falconbridge spokeswoman Caroline Casselman said the company was assessing its inventory levels and would meet its customer commitments. She said Falconbridge had not built up inventories in anticipation of a work stoppage.
"We're six hours into a strike, so it's a little early to be talking about long-term impact," Casselman said in a telephone interview.
Falconbridge has forecast total nickel output of 220 million pounds in 1997.
Research Capital Corp. analyst Manford Mallory said the strike "could play out very much like the Inco situation."
"I'd be surprised if this was settled very quickly in the next couple of days," he said. "I think the short scenario is for a couple of weeks, but these things are unpredictable."
Inco, the Western world's biggest nickel producer, said last week its strike shaved $20 million from its second-quarter earnings.
Inco also cut its estimated 1997 nickel output to 413 million pounds from a previous estimate of 430 million pounds.

But Inco's 26-day work stoppage did not have a significant impact on nickel prices, analysts said. They said Falconbridge's strike would have to last longer before it had a major effect on metal markets.
"Falconbridge's operations in Sudbury are about half the size of Inco's. So if they are off a couple of months, then it could have a meaningful impact," Mallory said.
Falconbridge stock fell 50 cents Canadian to C$29.10 on the Toronto Stock Exchange.
